subject: Science
title: Why day turns to night
objective_verbatim: Explain day and night and the apparent movement of the Sun.
reading_age_est: rough ARI grade 2.61 on 877 pupil-visible words; heuristic age guide 8.61 years, not a formal reading-age test
pupil_words: Show why day turns to night and why the Sun seems to move.
success_criteria: I can point to the day and night sides.
I can turn the model and explain when night comes.
I can explain why the Sun seems to move.

vocab.example: Earth’s rotation brings day and night.

vocab.definition: an imagined line a planet spins around
an area where an object blocks light
vocab.example: The ball makes a shadow on the desk.

vocab.definition: a curved path around another object
vocab.example: Earth’s orbit takes it around the Sun.

retrieval.question: Name one mechanism from our forces work.
Name one force from our first science week.

stages.pupil_text: Place a dot on the ball. Point to the side lit by the torch.
stages.adult_text: Offer a seat or standing spot. End with a one-minute reset.

stages.pupil_text: Think back. Say, point or write one answer for each question.
stages.adult_text: Ask three low-stakes questions without a public test.

stages.pupil_text: Watch: the torch stays still. I turn the ball. The dot has day when it faces the light. It has night when it faces away.
stages.adult_text: Model the full sequence. Keep light out of eyes. Ask the show-me check.

stages.pupil_text: Now try the same model. Two steps are done. Complete the last step: turn the dot away and name what comes next.
stages.adult_text: Wait for the missing step. End with a one-minute reset.

stages.pupil_text: Turn the ball. Choose where the dot is when it is night. Show your choice with the group.
stages.adult_text: Use an all-pupil hinge response and the decision rule in the note.

stages.pupil_text: Show day and night at the dot. Explain why the Sun seems to move, even when our torch stays still.
stages.adult_text: One adult supports agreed pupils, the other holds the group; swap across the week. One-minute reset at end.

stages.pupil_text: Tell a partner what your model shows. Hear one comment. Change one part and say what you changed.
stages.adult_text: Give one specific comment, invite a self-edit (//) or read-back (?).

stages.pupil_text: Show how you know. Tell us your feedback and next step. Say, point, sign, draw or write.
stages.adult_text: Hear answer, choose next model or help; hand over highest prompt and independent part.

worked_example.full: Torch still → dot faces the torch: day → turn the ball → dot faces away: night. Earth’s rotation makes the Sun seem to move.
worked_example.faded: Torch still → dot faces the torch: day → turn the ball → dot faces away: ____.
worked_example.removed_step: Name night when the dot faces away from the torch.
worked_example.fade_next: Next time omit the day label too; ask pupils to name both positions before word cards.

cfu.question: Show me: where is the dot when that place has day?
cfu.answer: On the side facing the torch or light.

hinge.question: On a new ball model, the red dot has just turned from light into shade. What does the shade represent?

options.diagnosis: Keeps the old day label after the dot has rotated into shade.
Treats darkness at one place as the Sun switching off.
Extends one dot’s night to every place on Earth.

hinge.decision_rule: About 3 in 4 or more right → move on. Otherwise re-model with the dot on the far side of the ball, then ask the parallel hinge.
hinge.parallel_hinge: A blue dot turns from shade into torchlight. Which part of a day does this represent? Answer: daytime at that dot.

misconceptions.misconception: Night at one dot means night everywhere on Earth.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses C, “The whole Earth going dark.”
misconceptions.correction: Turn the ball: one dot can be in shade while another still faces the light.

misconceptions.misconception: The Sun switches off when our place has night.
misconceptions.spot: Pupil chooses B, “The Sun turning off now.”
misconceptions.correction: Keep the torch on and turn the ball; the dot moves into shade.

we_do.support: Point to the torch and dot before naming the missing step.
we_do.stretch: Explain why the torch need not move to change the view at the dot.
we_do.F: Point to the torch and dot before naming the missing step.
we_do.M: Fill the blank and explain why.
we_do.H: Explain why the torch need not move to change the view at the dot.

tiers.F: Point to the lit side and the dark side.
tiers.M: Explain what the dot sees as Earth turns.
tiers.H: Explain why the Sun seems to move across our sky while the model torch stays still.

stems.F: I point to ___ for day and ___ for night.
stems.M: The dot has night when ___ because ___.
stems.H: The Sun seems to move because ___. The model shows ___.

tiers.go_deeper: Mark two dots on opposite sides. Explain why one has day while the other has night.
tiers.early_finisher: Two dots, one turn: test the claim that the Sun goes round Earth each day. Show the motion that explains both dots. Name one limit of the torch model.

adaptations.cognition_learning: Use a three-step dot and torch card. Omit its last word, then fade the card.
adaptations.communication_interaction: Point to the model before a partner rehearsal with the M or H speaking frame.
adaptations.semh: Offer a known kit role, a quiet pause cue and one small re-entry step.
adaptations.sensory_physical: Use a stable stand or a large tactile dot; a photo can capture a genuine demonstration.
adaptations.eal: Pre-teach science words with the diagram. Plan in any language; use M or H speaking frame before writing. EAL is language access, not a reason to move down to F.

speaking_frames: The dot has night when ___ because ___.
The Sun seems to move because ___; the model shows ___.

ta_focus.i_do: Watch the dot. Point to it when it faces the light.
ta_focus.we_do: What is done already? What step is left for you?
ta_focus.independent: Show your first step. What can you do on your own next?

prompt_ladder: Point to the dot or light.
Ask: What changes at the dot?
Model one turn; let the pupil try.
Finish one example together, then return the next turn to the pupil.

F.q: Point to day on the model.

M.q: Why does the dot get night?
M.a: It turns away from the light.

H.q: Why does the Sun seem to cross the sky?
What does the torch model leave out?
H.a: It simplifies size, distance and Earth’s orbit.

items: Dot faces away: choose day or night

interactions.answer_key: D. Night at the red dot. Teacher reads group response; no automatic grade.
interactions.question: On a new ball model, the red dot has just turned from light into shade. What does the shade represent?

diagrams.alt: Simple model: light from the Sun reaches the left side of Earth. A dot on that side has day; a dot away from light has night. The line through Earth is its axis.
diagrams.caption: Light reaches one side of Earth. This model is simplified and not to scale.

practical.prediction: Predict: if the dot turns away from the torch, will it have day or night?
method: Place the dot on the ball.
Keep the torch still and aim it at the ball, away from eyes.
Turn the dot to face the torch; record day or night.
Turn the dot away; record day or night.
results_table: Dot faces the torch | day or night?
Dot faces away | day or night?
practical.risk: Check against the school risk assessment and CLEAPSS guidance. Do not shine the torch into eyes.
practical.pupil_risk: Torch beams can dazzle eyes; a loose ball may roll away.
practical.pupil_safety: Aim the torch at the ball, never at eyes. Keep the ball on the tray or stand.

facts.claim: Earth rotates on an axis; its daily turn causes the day and night cycle.
Earth has day on its side facing the Sun and night on the side facing away.
Earth’s turn makes the Sun seem to move across the sky.
Earth orbits the Sun; orbit is a curved path around another object.
facts.source: NASA Science, Facts About Earth, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/; NASA Space Place, Glossary, https://spaceplace.nasa.gov/glossary/en/

facts.claim: Rotation is a turn about an axis; Earth’s axis is an imagined line through its poles.
facts.source: NASA Science, Facts About Earth, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/; NASA Science, Earth spin axis, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/climate-change/scientists-id-three-causes-of-earths-spin-axis-drift/

facts.claim: A shadow forms where an object blocks light.
Earlier SoW rows cover Moon around Earth, mechanisms and named forces.
facts.source: GROW SOW 2026-27-2.xlsx, GROW Weekly - Autumn!C32, C35, C38

facts.claim: SVG labels Sun, light, Earth, axis, day, night and its simplified geometry show the day and night model.
facts.source: NASA Science, Heliophysics Big Idea 1.1, https://science.nasa.gov/learn/heat/big-ideas/big-idea-1-1/; NASA Science, Earth spin axis, https://science.nasa.gov/earth/climate-change/scientists-id-three-causes-of-earths-spin-axis-drift/
